misconception_description: Student believes that conditional statements, i.e., Python statements that evaluate to either True or False, must be explicitly compared to True or False to be used in conditionals.

solutions.generated_code:
program HitungInversi
kamus
  a, b, c, jumlah : integer
algoritma
  input(a, b, c)
  jumlah <- 0
  if (a > b) == true then
    jumlah <- jumlah + 1
  endif
  if (a > c) == true then
    jumlah <- jumlah + 1
  endif
  if (b > c) == true then
    jumlah <- jumlah + 1
  endif
  output(jumlah)
endprogram

metadata.modification_notes: The student adds an explicit '== True' comparison to the conditional statement in the if block. The student believes that the comparison expression (arr[i] > arr[j]) must be explicitly compared to True to be used in an if statement. While this is redundant and not Pythonic, the code functions correctly because (arr[i] > arr[j]) evaluates to a boolean, and comparing it to True yields the same boolean value. This is purely a stylistic issue that demonstrates a misunderstanding of how Python evaluates conditions, but does not introduce any logical errors.
